title: All stage classes are not equal in their effects on population growth
abstract_text: Abstract Understanding the effects of stage structure on population processes is critical for wildlife population ecologists, both because different stages are important to conservation management decision-makers and because structure affects population growth in profound ways. Matrix population models account for stage structure with straightforward links to vital rates measured in the field. Reproductive values capture the fact that different stages are not equal in their influence on population growth, and can therefore help inform actions ranging from translocations to harvest strategies. If vital rates remain relatively constant over time, a population will achieve a stable stage distribution (SSD) and an asymptotic population growth rate (λSSD) characteristic of those vital rates. However, if vital rates or number of individuals in different stages change, transient dynamics can produce wildly erratic fluctuations even under constant environmental conditions. Different stage-specific vital rates have different infinitesimal influence on population growth rate (measured by analytical sensitivity and elasticity), and they also differ in how much they vary and covary with each other. The broad field of sensitivity analysis quantifies the relative importance of different vital rates and their variance, and how different management actions would affect population growth or persistence. Manual perturbations can identify the relative efficiency of specific management actions affecting particular vital rates. Life-stage simulation analysis (LSA) simulates many possible matrices from user-specified means and variances to provide direct insight (beyond elasticity) into how management-induced changes in certain vital rates are expected to affect population growth.

title: Preface to Second Edition
abstract_text: In the 6 years since the first edition of this book, wildlife population ecology has become even more central in conservation decision-making, and has fully matured into a rigorous science. My goal with this second edition is to track the successes and maturation of the field. I have tried to retain the core concepts and readability that have made this book successful and useful for practitioners and students, while updating the text with many of the astonishing developments of the past decade. To that end, I have endeavored to retain that readability and breadth in this edition, while incorporating the considerable changes and ever-deepening insights since this book went to press in 2006. I have added more than 225 new references, including 181 published since 2006, and substantially revised all chapters. Examples outside the US have been especially emphasized. A partial list of some of the most substantial expansions and additions in this edition includes: key concepts in hypothesis testing and information theoretic approaches; new advances in genomics and gene expression; estimating trend from real field data; dealing with correlations over time and among vital rates in population dynamics; consequences of population inertia; Allee effects critical to population persistence; linking population dynamics to fitness measures; examples of ecological traps and source sink dynamics; separating component versus population-level effects on inbreeding depression, genetic rescue, and density dependence; estimation and interpretation of connectivity among populations; expanded coverage of climate change and other deterministic human-caused stressors; and updates in risk assessment and harvest management. I have switched the order of Chapter 6 (density dependence) and 7 (effects of age and stage structure on population dynamics) to better frame the ways that density dependence interacts with stage structure to affect population dynamics.

title: Predation and wildlife populations
abstract_text: Abstract Whether or not predators affect population dynamics of their prey is of huge societal interest, and can be understood with three fundamental principles of wildlife population ecology. First, the predation rate is a function of how predator numbers change with prey numbers (numerical response) and the number of prey killed by each predator (functional response). Multiple predator species can complicate the numerical and functional responses in several ways that affect conservation management decisions. These include trophic cascades and apparent competition. A functional response of predator kills well beyond energetic needs, surplus killing, can emerge as an evolutionary byproduct of a predator learning how to successfully kill. Certain types of functional responses can create Allee effects in small prey populations which can spiral endangered species toward extinction. The second key factor affecting whether predators will control prey numbers is whether the predation mortality is compensatory, whereby predation has no effect on overall survival because predator removals are replaced by reduced mortality from other sources, or from increased reproduction or immigration. Alternatively, if predation mortality is additive then survival declines linearly as predation increases. The third driver of predator effects on prey is how different age or stage classes of prey are differentially vulnerable to being killed and have different effects on prey population growth rate. An additional consideration is how predators may affect prey by creating a landscape of fear through non-consumptive effects on prey behavior, movements, and stress levels with potential effects on population-level fitness and dynamics.

title: Preface to Third Edition
abstract_text: The aim of this book is to provide students and professionals a hard-nosed, science-based foundation for positive actions to nurture wildlife conservation on a changing planet. It draws from broadly overlapping fields of applied population ecology and population biology - which themselves intersect disciplines across field biology, ecology, evolution, genetics, and quantitative modeling. We extract from that cross-cutting science the foundations of rigorous mindset and applied tools to illuminate the dynamics of wild animal populations in a changing world, and to support practical evaluation of how real-world actions can most effectively affect conservation outcomes. This is the third edition, but it’s so updated and revised that it’s more like a new birth. L.S. Mills published the first edition of ‘Conservation of Wildlife Populations: Demography, Genetics, and Management’ in 2006. Mills’ 2013 second edition carried the same title, with revision of references, expansion of international scope, and increased breadth and depth.

title: Density-dependent population change
abstract_text: Abstract Density of conspecifics can be a major driver of population dynamics, with implications ranging from management of endangered species to harvest strategy assessment. Traditionally most focus has been on negative density dependence, whereby increasing abundance has negative effects on survival and reproduction due to competition, predation, and disease. The simplest way to model negative density dependence is with the logistic growth function, which imposes a linear decrease in the realized population growth rate as the population increases from very small numbers to a carrying capacity where the population becomes stationary. The logistic equation has been useful as a conceptually simple distillation of complexity and in showing how negative density dependence with time lags can lead to non-intuitive outcomes such as limit cycles and chaotic dynamics. However, the logistic can also be blamed for decades of overharvest of wild populations due to an overemphasis on maximum sustained yield at 1/2 of carrying capacity. Importantly density is not just a negative force on population growth; in many cases, survival and birth rates can decrease as abundance decreases (positive density dependence) that can drive extinctions. These effects at small abundances, called Allee effects, can result from breakdowns in mating behaviors, modification of habitats, or cooperative defense. Finally, density might act on component vital rates in populations, but what really matters for conservation is whether those component vital rates translate into ensemble changes to population growth rate.

title: Genetic concepts and tools to support wildlife population ecology
abstract_text: Abstract Describing, measuring, and interpreting genetic variation has become critical to the science behind the conservation of wildlife populations. This became especially true with the development of PCR (polymerase chain reaction), which opened the door to analyses of unfathomably old or vanishingly tiny tissue samples that could be obtained noninvasively. These innovations launched a subfield called environmental DNA (eDNA) for extracting genetic information for multiple species from samples as small as a single drop of water or a flake of sloughed skin. Genetic variation based on mitochondrial and nuclear DNA can be determined with a variety of markers, including metabarcoding, microsatellites, and single nucleotide polymorphisms. Most recently, high-throughput sequencing has allowed evaluation of large portions of the genome and identification of the genetic basis of traits under selection in a changing world (functional genomics and transcriptomics). Functional genomics promises to open new doors for wildlife population ecology as we come to understand the genetic basis of traits of management or evolutionary importance. Although the main purpose of this chapter is to provide the fundamentals of genetics and tools that underlie genetic concepts and applications found throughout this book, we focus here on a few key applications such as determination of the hybrid status or taxonomic affiliation of species and subspecies units. DNA markers can help determine evolutionarily significant units, distinct population segments, and management units. Further, the extent of hybridization, and its role in providing potential sources of adaptive variation in a changing world, can now be better understood and appreciated.

title: Exponential (or geometric) change
abstract_text: Abstract When a wildlife population’s trajectory over time is unaffected by its own density or other individual-level attributes, its trend is considered to be exponential (described by λ) or geometric (described by r). Although estimating the average exponential trend is important, applied population ecology must also grapple with the causes and consequences of variation in the trajectory over time. Sometimes the variation over time is an illusion or nuisance arising from sample variance that arises inevitably from the processing of estimating abundance in a time series. By contrast, the deterministic and stochastic factors (which include demographic stochasticity and environmental stochasticity) that cause random year-to-year changes in abundance each year lead to process variance in the trajectory. Process variance depresses the long-term most likely abundance relative to mean expected abundance based on the arithmetic average growth rate, leading to the counterintuitive and deeply conservation-relevant outcome that a population with a fluctuating positive growth rate may actually be most likely to decline. The relatively simple and traditional ways to estimate trend and its variance from field-based time series typically do not account for the variation that arises from both sample variance in the abundance estimates and from process noise. Because both forms of variation typically occur in time series of wild populations, the best exponential trend estimator accommodates both sampling and process variance via a state space model. Although no population can continue to grow without limit, simple exponential change forms the basis for more complicated models of population growth.

title: Preface to First Edition
abstract_text: Population biology spans the wide and fascinating world of population ecology, demography, and population genetics. This book extracts from these fields the most relevant concepts and principles for solving real-world management problems in wildlife and conservation biology. It will build on your training in basic ecology and genetics, then move deeper into areas where ecological and genetic concepts and theory are applied. Because this is an applied book on population biology, it will not derive or prove theoretical premises, nor will it dwell on theory not directly applicable to management problems. There are already excellent books that cover basic ecology, theoretical and mathematical population biology, and conservation genetics. There are also excellent books describing case studies of wildlife management and conservation practice. With this book, I hope to fill in the space between these texts, providing a conceptual framework spanning from fieldwork to demographic models and genetic analysis as they inform applied decision-making.

title: Dynamics of multiple populations
abstract_text: Abstract Dispersal and gene flow into and out of populations—broadly called connectivity—fundamentally shape wildlife distribution and abundance across a landscape. Connectivity determines taxonomic distinctiveness, colonization of new sites in a changing environment, and multi-population persistence. A dazzling array of technology and computational techniques exist to estimate movement rates and to separate genetic connectivity via gene flow (dependent on the absolute number of migrants per generation) from demographic connectivity (based on how immigration and emigration compare to local births and deaths). The fate of a set of isolated populations will depend on both population-specific extinction probabilities and on the correlation among their dynamics due to shared environments. If populations are distributed as a metapopulation, persistence becomes a question of weighing within-population vital rates (births and deaths) against among-population rates (immigration and emigration). Source populations that contribute to metapopulation persistence can be distinguished (using the contribution metric) from sinks that drain the metapopulation. The most insidious sinks are ecological traps, with cues that attract animals but then lead to depressed vital rates. To restore fragmented connectivity in a landscape, corridors are one option, as is modifying the intervening matrix that originally broke up the connectivity. As a last resort, physical translocations might be necessary, while applying a broad set of population ecology principles centered on demography, genetics, and behavior to determine the optimal donor population, number of individuals to translocate, and their individual characteristics.

title: Sustainable harvest principles, models, and best practices
abstract_text: Abstract Harvest of wild species is central to human existence. Wildlife population ecology principles can inform how many and which types of animals can be removed under sustained yield management that avoids unacceptable declines in the harvested population over time. The effects of harvest in any particular instance are informed by knowledge of the harvest rate, which age or stages are being killed, and the degree to which harvest can be compensated for by changes in mortality or other vital rates. Because harvest is just one of many interacting factors affecting population dynamics means that active adaptive management is required to determine the harvest effects. Population models can account for the fact that all ages and stages of animals are not created equal in either their access or appeal to hunters, or in their effects on population dynamics. Although a harvest-initiated sex-ratio skew toward males can increase population growth, too strong a skew can decrease reproduction and increase mortality. Also, strong harvest-induced selection on animals can drive evolved phenotypic changes in the population opposite of that desired. The full weight of applied population ecology joins with management constraints and political feasibility in structured decision-making (SDM) and adaptive harvest management (AHM). SDM and AHM explicitly embrace both the disparate values of people affected by harvest decisions and the uncertainty arising from biological mechanisms (scientific uncertainty), population status and trend (partial observability), and in the ability of harvest regulations to achieve particular outcomes (partial controllability).

title: Conservation of Wildlife Populations
abstract_text: Abstract Applied population ecology has matured into a sophisticated science with considerable potential to help conserve wild populations in a rapidly changing world. And yet, much of the practical power of wildlife population ecology has been isolated in specialized texts and so remains underappreciated. This third edition is a major revision of ‘Conservation of Wildlife Populations.’ It begins with core fundamentals of estimating, describing, and projecting dynamics of fluctuating populations, including varying responses across individuals, populations, species, and communities. It then covers the intersection of population dynamics with genetic structure, predation, inbreeding, climate change, population viability analysis, multiple population dynamics, structured decision-making, and harvest. Quantitative aspects and non-intuitive concepts are explained throughout with attention to clarity and applications. References and case studies have been thoroughly updated and expanded in global scope, and fish and fisheries are now included, but this third edition maintains its readable and approachable style with one voice (as opposed to edited volumes). By the end students should have the confidence to advance both conservation management and research by effectively using scientific data, models, and the literature to address pressing questions. At the same time, Conservation of Wildlife Populations (Third Edition) will provide to practitioners in the field—in one place and with plenty of practical examples—the scientific basis to make efficient and effective conservation decisions based on the latest advances in the ecological, evolutionary, and genetic aspects of population ecology.

title: The big picture
abstract_text: Abstract Applied wildlife population ecology has a vast body of insights to help reduce the collision between humans and the rest of biodiversity. Wildlife can be broadly defined as free-living, undomesticated vertebrate species (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fishes). Although only a small slice of the approximately 2 million named and described eukaryotic species comprising biodiversity on earth, wildlife are the species on which most public attention and conservation efforts focus, and are often strong interactors in human-dominated ecosystems. Biodiversity (and wildlife) benefit human needs and provide emotional and spiritual sustenance (biophilia). After >12,000 years of slow growth, human population growth rate accelerated tremendously in the 1800s until peaking in the 1960s. Although human numbers are now almost 8 billion, growth rates continue to decline mostly due to decreases in female fertility. By the end of this century, vital rates (birth and death rates) should be at replacement, implying a flat population trajectory, although population momentum will foster continued increase of about a billion more humans over several decades. Human numbers and per-individual impacts have reverberated across the planet, increasing extinction rates for the rest of biodiversity far above the baseline deep-time level and approaching the cusp of a mass extinction event and planetary transformation whose magnitude has earned the label of Anthropocene. And yet, history has shown that the marriage of wildlife population ecology science and heroic hard work have changed the trajectory of human-caused extinctions. Wildlife ecology can provide non-intuitive, science-based insights to underlie conservation successes on a changing planet.

title: Population responses to human-caused stressors: Move, adjust, or die
abstract_text: Abstract Deterministic human-caused stressors include habitat conversion, climate change, pollution, disease and other invasive species, and unregulated harvest. These stressors, often acting synergistically, can depress the functions or efficiencies of traits of individuals, which can decrease vital rates and λ. A widespread type of stressor generated by climate change involves a phenological mismatch between changing seasonal environmental conditions and the species’ annual life-history rhythms that evolved to track seasonal changes. Building on nearly all the applied population ecology concepts in the book, here we ask the big-picture question: How will wildlife population dynamics respond to new and accelerating stressors in a changing world (and what can we do about it)? Death and extinction are not inevitable; two other options could facilitate resilience such that populations can persist through change: animals could move (range shifts and altered migration routes) to escape the stressor; or they can stay in place and successfully locally adjust to maintain (or increase) λ. One way to rapidly adjust to changed conditions is phenotypic plasticity, whereby an individual expresses different forms of a trait under different conditions. Another way to adjust and persist is through adaptation, an increase in fitness arising from evolutionary change in gene frequencies driven by natural selection. If plasticity and/or adaptation are sufficient to reverse a declining population trajectory, then ecological or evolutionary rescue can occur. Four conditions that maximize local population persistence and rescue are discussed, with the most extreme (but potentially necessary) management options including directed evolution via synthetic biology.

title: Credits for Epigraphs
Genetic variation and fitness of wildlife populations
abstract_text: Abstract Genetic variation is a central concept in applied population ecology because it can shape everything from successful long-term adaptation to short-term population dynamics and persistence. This chapter first describes the four interacting drivers of genetic variation (natural selection, genetic drift, gene flow, and mutation); how the inbreeding coefficient captures inbreeding occurring from either preferential mating with relatives or—more commonly in wildlife populations—from a small effective population size (Ne); how and why inbreeding can lead to inbreeding depression in wild populations; and the potential for outbreeding depression. The rest of the chapter considers how inbreeding depression can affect λ; how genetic rescue can reverse population declines caused by inbreeding depression (being careful to separate effects of inbreeding depression and genetic rescue at the level of both component vital rates and population growth); and how gene flow at a level of 1–10 migrants per generation can reduce the accumulation of inbreeding due to drift while also maintaining local adaptations. A range of case studies at the end explores where the “rubber hits the road” at the intersection of genetic variation, demographic responses, and the realities of implementing conservation management actions.

title: Gaining reliable knowledge
abstract_text: Abstract Gaining reliable knowledge in applied wildlife population ecology requires a rigorous and formal process coupling ideas (hypotheses) to reliable measured facts. Some of the prerequisites to obtaining trustworthy facts include replication, randomization, and the use of controls. Accurate measurements have low bias and high precision. In the spirit of our “embrace uncertainty” mantra, variance may be more important than the mean. Natural history, intuition, and observed correlations form an important basis for hypothesis generation, but specific a priori predictions should then be tested against data. The traditional approach of testing for statistical significance using P-values and null hypotheses has been criticized for its reliance on an arbitrary threshold of P=0.05, a tendency to promote meaningless null hypotheses, and too little consideration of statistical power (a real problem when missing an effect could damage wildlife populations). Alternative multimodel selection frameworks using either maximum likelihood or Bayesian criteria have gained strong footholds in wildlife population biology because they allow for direct consideration of multiple hypotheses. Further, hierarchical models provide a framework representing population ecology hypotheses in mathematical terms, intersecting the biological processes of interest with observation models capturing how the data are obtained. Finally, any rigor in study design or implementation is bereft without a strong foundation in ethics. Scientific societies in applied wildlife population ecology have ethics guidelines, and we should all be familiar with them. The integrity of our profession depends on it.

title: Estimating population size and vital rates
abstract_text: Abstract Population size and vital rates form the skeleton upon which the body of population ecology hangs. Both population models and applied conservation management actions rest on estimates of abundance, survival, reproduction, and sex ratios (as well as population connectivity; Chapter 10). Indirect indices of abundance (e.g. snow tracks, call counts) are severely compromised because they confound change in true abundance (what we care about) with a change in the relationship between the index and true abundance. Direct estimation of abundance involves a count of animals divided by an estimated probability of detecting an animal during the count period. In rare circumstances, all animals are counted, a true census. In most cases, however, probability of detection is <1 and must be estimated with either unmarked methods or capture–mark–recapture (CMR) approaches (which increasingly rely on noninvasive methods including cameras and DNA genotyping). The current best practice for directly estimating density (abundance/area) from CMR data uses spatial capture–recapture (SCR) approaches. A different alternative to indices when abundance estimation is not feasible tracks the occupancy of a species. Survival estimates include models that assume known fate or use recorded deaths (band-return models) or recorded live marked animals (Cormack–Jolly–Seber models). These approaches can be mixed and matched, but the commonality is to avoid the naïve estimator of survival (number encountered/total), which ignores the fact that animals not captured or sighted may be alive but simply not detected. Sex ratio is essentially the ratio of female to male abundances, estimated through statistical methods.

Influence of habitat attributes on terrestrial orchid communities across a tropical forest recovery gradient
abstract_text: Understanding drivers of plant diversity and distributions is critical for their conservation, particularly among changing environments. While plants’ responses to disturbances are relatively well-studied, in-depth analyses of how they respond to habitat recovery are surprisingly scarce. This is particularly true for one of the most diverse, sensitive, and threatened plant families: the Orchidaceae. To address this knowledge gap, we evaluated the diversity and distribution of terrestrial orchid species within a recovering tropical forest landscape in the Republic of Palau. We tested the hypotheses that orchid abundance, richness, and diversity vary across a forest successional gradient and that orchid species exhibit specificity and/or fidelity to particular tree species. Surveys yielded distribution data for 23 orchid species and General Linear Models revealed that habitat type and tree abundance, diversity, and size significantly affected orchid abundance. Habitat type and tree abundance also affected orchid richness and diversity. Indicator analysis showed that only two orchid species were significantly associated with individual tree species. The local landscape-scale study established that orchid communities varied across habitats and that mature forests had greater orchid abundance, richness, and diversity. Interestingly, tree abundance had a stronger influence on orchid communities than tree diversity, tree size, or specific tree species. The study demonstrated that orchids can occupy a range of successional habitats and indicated that reservation strategies paired with restoration efforts utilizing various tree species for reforestation will benefit orchid communities over potentially shorter timeframes than might occur without active management.

title: Diversity and genetic structure of kanisté (Pouteria campechiana), an underutilized tropical fruit tree native to the Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico
source_name: Journal of Agriculture and Food Research
abstract_text: ABSTRACT Fruit trees have been part of human diet since the dawn of humanity. Kanisté ( Pouteria campechiana , Sapotaceae), is an underutilized fruit tree native to Mesoamerica. In the Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico, its consumption and cultivation by Mayan communities have declined in recent decades, placing this species at potential risk. The objectives of this study were to evaluate the genetic diversity and structure of kanisté within its natural distribution area and possible center of domestication. To this end, young leaves from 40 trees were collected from natural and anthropogenic environments and characterized using 18 microsatellite (SSR) markers and 167 Inter-Simple Sequence Repeat (ISSR) loci. Additionally, we conducted a BLAST analysis to explore potential associations between the SSR loci and phenotypic traits. Results from both molecular markers revealed two main genetic groups with substructures related to the geographical origins of individuals collected in natural vegetation. At the species level, genetic diversity was moderate (SSR: H E =0.52±0.031), but higher in the natural habitats (SSR: H E =0.64±0.032) than in anthropogenic environments (SSR: H E =0.39±0.058). While these results may indicate a good conservation status of the species in its natural range, they could also reflect the effects of genetic erosion on cultivated kanisté, raising concerns for its long-term viability. Notably, 16 of the 18 SSR loci exhibited hits on protein-coding regions, including genes involved in regulating sugar flux and seed development. This study provides a foundation for future conservation and management strategies for kanisté in the Yucatán Peninsula and opens new avenues for research on domestication and genetics conservation.

title: Emerging Invasive Weeds in Iran: Occurrence, Ecological Impacts, and Sustainable Management
abstract_text: Invasive weeds pose a growing threat to global biodiversity, ecosystem stability, and agricultural productivity with significant ecological and economic consequences. In Iran, the rapid spread of invasive species such as Boreava orientalis, Azolla spp., Ibicella lutea, Physalis divaricata, Picnomon acarna, Cynanchum acutum, Vicia hyrcanica, Eichhornia crassipes, and Ambrosia psilostachya has severely affected native ecosystems, disrupted ecological processes, and threatened food security. These species exhibit aggressive traits such as rapid maturity, high reproductive rates, seed dormancy, and allelopathy that enable them to outcompete native species and successfully invade and dominate delicate habitats. Despite their documented impacts, a critical gap remains in understanding their biology, ecology, and management, particularly in understudied regions like Iran. This review synthesizes current knowledge on major invasive weeds affecting Iranian agroecosystems, with a focus on their ecological impacts and the urgent need for sustainable management strategies. It presents an integrated framework that combines ecological, biological, and management perspectives to address invasiveness, particularly in highly adaptable species like B. orientalis and A. psilostachya. This review highlights the critical role of interdisciplinary collaboration, advanced technology, and community involvement in developing effective strategies. It offers practical guidance for researchers, policymakers, and agricultural stakeholders, serving as a model for managing invasive species in other vulnerable regions. Ultimately, it supports global efforts to safeguard biodiversity, improve crop productivity, and strengthen ecological resilience against the growing threat of invasive species.

title: Migration Patterns of Epiphyllous Bryophyte Metapopulations in Amazonian Fragmented Landscape Inferred From Census and Genomic Data
abstract_text: ABSTRACT Habitat fragmentation affects metapopulation dynamics by reducing patch (discrete area occupied by a local population) size and connectivity, but its long‐term genetic consequences are confounded by species‐specific traits and limitations of sequencing techniques. Studies of terrestrial plants with relatively short generation times, combined with high‐throughput sequencing, provide valuable insights into the demographic and genetic effects of land‐use change. We integrate long‐term censuses and genotyping data from epiphyllous bryophyte metapopulations in experimentally fragmented Amazonian forests. We focused on two bryophyte species with contrasting mating systems across 11 populations in small (1‐ and 10‐ha) and large (100‐ha and continuous) habitats. We aim to assess how long‐term reductions in colony numbers in small fragments affect population genetic diversity and differentiation compared to larger habitats. We also explore how species' mating systems influence migration patterns across forest sites, with bisexual species expected to exhibit a higher likelihood of sexual reproduction and spore output than their unisexual counterparts. Our results reveal contrasting patterns of genetic structure between the two species, with no consistent effects of forest fragmentation detected across the landscape. The bisexual species showed notably lower genetic diversity and slightly higher differentiation in small fragments, suggesting a non‐equilibrium metapopulation driven by limited migration. In contrast, the unisexual species exhibited minimal genetic impact from fragmentation, maintaining symmetrical migration among fragments regardless of size, indicative of patchy metapopulation dynamics. This study highlights how contrasting mating systems in epiphyllous bryophytes influence migration patterns and underscores the species‐specific responses to habitat fragmentation.
